question: What are the main concepts of OOP?
answer:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is structured around four primary pillars designed to maximize code reusability, modularity, and maintainability:


1. Encapsulation

Concept: Bundles data (attributes) and the functions (methods) that operate on that data into a single unit (a class), while restricting direct access to internal components.

Mechanism: Implemented using access modifiers (private, protected, public) and controlled through getter and setter methods.

Purpose: Prevents accidental modification of internal state and ensures data integrity.

Example: A BankAccount class keeps the balance property private. External code cannot directly do account.balance = 500000 and must go through a validated withdraw() or deposit() method.


2. Abstraction

Concept: Hides complex underlying implementation details and exposes only the essential interface necessary for the user to interact with an object.

Mechanism: Implemented using abstract classes, interfaces, and protocol definitions.

Purpose: Reduces cognitive complexity and decouples the interface from the underlying execution.

Example: A smartphone provides a simple “Send” button on a messaging app without requiring you to understand network packet headers, socket connections, or encryption protocols happening behind the scenes.


3. Inheritance

Concept: Allows a new class (subclass or child class) to inherit state and behaviors from an existing class (superclass or parent class), modeling an “is-a” relationship.

Mechanism: Subclasses extend base classes, automatically gaining their non-private properties and methods.

Purpose: Eliminates code duplication and establishes structured hierarchies.

Example: A generic Vehicle base class defines properties like speed and methods like move(). A derived ElectricCar class inherits these automatically while adding distinct properties like batteryPercentage.


4. Polymorphism

Concept: The ability of different classes to respond to the same interface or method call in distinct ways (“many forms”).

Types:

  • Compile-Time (Static): Method overloading (same method name with different parameters) or operator overloading.
  • Runtime (Dynamic): Method overriding, where a subclass provides its own specific implementation of a method already defined in its parent class (dynamic dispatch).

Purpose: Allows systems to write generic code that can operate on diverse subclasses interchangeably.

Example: A base class Shape defines a calculateArea() method. Subclasses Circle, Rectangle, and Triangle each implement their own distinct mathematical formulas for calculateArea(), but can all be stored and evaluated in the same Shape[] collection.


PrinciplePrimary FocusKey Mechanism
EncapsulationData protection & scopingAccess modifiers, getters/setters
AbstractionComplexity hiding & clarityInterfaces, abstract classes
InheritanceCode reuse & taxonomyClass extension (is-a relationships)
PolymorphismFlexibility & interchangeabilityMethod overriding & overloading

question: Abstract class vs interface?
answer:
Both abstract classes and interfaces define contracts and enable polymorphism, but they serve different architectural purposes and have distinct capabilities:


Abstract Class

Concept: A class that cannot be instantiated directly and may contain a mix of abstract (unimplemented) and concrete (implemented) methods, along with instance fields and constructors.

Use When: Multiple related classes share common state or behaviour (true is-a relationship). A base class that needs to hold shared fields like createdAt, id, or common template logic.

Limitation: A class can extend only one abstract class (single inheritance).


Interface

Concept: A pure contract defining what a class must do, not how. Supports multiple implementation, enabling a class to implement many interfaces simultaneously.

Modern Java (8+) additions:

  • default methods — provide optional method implementations without breaking existing implementors.
  • static methods — utility/helper methods scoped to the interface.
  • private methods (Java 9+) — internal helper logic within the interface.

FeatureAbstract ClassInterface
Instance Fields✅ Yes❌ No (only constants)
Constructors✅ Yes❌ No
Multiple Inheritance❌ Single only✅ Multiple interfaces
Default Methods✅ Concrete methods✅ Since Java 8
Best Used ForShared base state & behaviorCapabilities & contracts

Rule of Thumb: Prefer interfaces for defining capabilities (Serializable, Comparable, Runnable). Use abstract classes when sharing common state or providing a template method pattern.

question: Difference between == and equals()?
answer:
This is one of the most common Java traps. The distinction depends on whether you are comparing primitives or objects:


== Operator

  • Primitives: Compares actual values. 5 == 5 is true.
  • Objects: Compares memory references (heap addresses). Two distinct objects with identical content will return false with ==.

equals() Method

  • Compares logical / content equality when properly overridden by the class.
  • Default implementation in Object behaves like == (reference comparison), so classes must override it for meaningful equality.
  • String, Integer, and all value-type wrappers override equals() correctly.

String a = new String("hello");
String b = new String("hello");

System.out.println(a == b);        // false — different heap objects
System.out.println(a.equals(b));   // true  — same content

// String Pool optimization (literals):
String x = "hello";
String y = "hello";
System.out.println(x == y);        // true  — same String pool reference

Aspect==equals()
PrimitivesCompares valuesN/A (autoboxed to objects)
ObjectsCompares heap referencesCompares logical content
Overridable❌ No✅ Yes (recommended)

question: Why override hashCode() with equals()?
answer:
This is a critical Java contract that, when violated, causes subtle, hard-to-debug bugs in collections like HashMap, HashSet, and Hashtable.


The Contract (from java.lang.Object):

  • If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() must also be true.
  • If a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(), a.equals(b) may or may not be true (collision is OK).

Why does it matter in HashMap?

  1. HashMap.put(key, value) first calls key.hashCode() to determine which bucket to place the entry.
  2. On HashMap.get(key), it again calls hashCode() to find the bucket, then uses equals() to locate the exact key within the bucket.
  3. If you override equals() but not hashCode(), two logically equal objects may hash to different buckets, so get() returns null even when the key was previously put.

// BROKEN — equals overridden, hashCode not:
Map<Point, String> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put(new Point(1, 2), "origin");
map.get(new Point(1, 2)); // Returns null! Different hashCode → different bucket

// CORRECT — both overridden:
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) { ... }
@Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }

Best Practice: Use Objects.hash(field1, field2, ...) or IDE-generated hashCode() to avoid manual mistakes. In Java 16+, use record types which auto-generate both correctly.

question: Why is String immutable?
answer:
String in Java is immutable — once created, its internal character array cannot be changed. This was a deliberate design decision in Java for multiple important reasons:


1. String Pool Optimization

The JVM maintains a String Constant Pool in the heap. When two variables hold the same string literal, they can safely share the same pool object because neither can alter it. This avoids redundant object creation and saves significant memory.

String a = "hello"; // Added to pool
String b = "hello"; // Reuses same pool object
System.out.println(a == b); // true — same reference

2. Thread Safety

Because String state can never change after construction, it is inherently thread-safe. Multiple threads can share and read the same String instance without synchronization.


3. Hash Code Caching

String.hashCode() is lazily computed on first call and then cached in a field. Since the value can never change, the cached hash is always valid — enabling String to be an extremely efficient HashMap key.


4. Security

Class loading, file paths, network connections, and database credentials rely on String parameters. If String were mutable, malicious code could modify these values after a security check but before the actual operation.


Important: Operations like concat(), toUpperCase(), and + do NOT modify the original — they return a new String object. Use StringBuilder for efficient repeated modifications in loops.

question: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?
answer:
All three represent character sequences, but differ in mutability and thread safety:


String — Immutable

Every modification (concatenation, replace, substring) produces a new String object. Chaining many + operations in a loop creates excessive garbage objects, degrading performance.

// BAD — creates N intermediate String objects:
String result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    result += i; // Creates a new String each time!
}

StringBuilder — Mutable, Not Thread-Safe

Maintains an internal mutable character buffer. Appending to a StringBuilder modifies it in place — no new objects. The default and recommended choice for string building in single-threaded contexts.

// GOOD — single buffer, O(n) total:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    sb.append(i);
}
String result = sb.toString();

StringBuffer — Mutable, Thread-Safe

Identical to StringBuilder API, but all methods are synchronized. Safe for use across multiple threads, but the synchronization overhead makes it slower than StringBuilder in single-threaded code. Rarely needed — prefer concurrent-specific structures instead.


PropertyStringStringBuilderStringBuffer
Mutable❌ No✅ Yes✅ Yes
Thread-Safe✅ Yes (immutable)❌ No✅ Yes (synchronized)
PerformanceSlow for concatenationFast ✅Slower (sync overhead)
Use CaseFixed text, keysSingle-thread buildingMulti-thread shared (rare)

question: How does HashMap work internally?
answer:
HashMap is a hash table implementation of the Map interface that provides average O(1) time complexity for get() and put() operations. Understanding its internals is crucial for writing efficient Java.


Internal Structure

Internally, a HashMap maintains an array of buckets (Node[] table). Each bucket can hold a linked list (or tree) of entries that hash to the same index.


Step-by-Step: How put(key, value) Works

  1. Compute Hash: hash = key.hashCode() is computed and further spread with a secondary bit-mixing operation to reduce clustering.
  2. Determine Bucket Index: index = hash & (capacity - 1). For a 16-bucket table, this selects one of 16 positions.
  3. Handle Collision: If a bucket already has an entry, the new entry is appended to the linked list in that bucket.
  4. Treeify (Java 8+): When a single bucket grows beyond 8 entries, the linked list is automatically converted to a Red-Black Tree for O(log n) worst-case lookup within that bucket.
  5. Resize (Rehash): When the total entry count exceeds capacity × loadFactor (default 0.75), the table doubles in size and all entries are rehashed.

Step-by-Step: How get(key) Works

  1. Compute hash of the key.
  2. Find the bucket index.
  3. Walk the linked list/tree in that bucket, calling equals() to find an exact key match.
  4. Return the associated value, or null if not found.

OperationAverage CaseWorst Case (all collide)
get() / put()O(1)O(log n) after treeify
Resize/RehashO(n)O(n)

Key Insight: Always override both hashCode() and equals() for custom key objects. A poor hashCode() (e.g., always returning 1) degrades HashMap performance to O(n) as all keys pile into one bucket.

question: What if two keys have the same hash code?
answer:
This scenario is called a Hash Collision. It is expected and handled by HashMap using a technique called Separate Chaining.


What Happens on Collision

  1. Both keys compute the same bucket index via their hash code.
  2. HashMap does not overwrite the existing entry — it appends the new entry as the next node in a linked list within that bucket.
  3. On get(key), after finding the bucket, HashMap walks the linked list and uses equals() to find the exact matching key.

// Both keys collide — same bucket, different equals():
map.put(new Key("A"), "value1"); // hashCode = 42
map.put(new Key("B"), "value2"); // hashCode = 42 (collision!)
// Bucket 42 now: [Key("A") → value1] → [Key("B") → value2]

When Collisions Degrade Performance

  • Each collision adds another node to the chain — lookup in a bucket degrades to O(n) in the worst case.
  • Java 8+ mitigation: When a single bucket grows beyond 8 entries, the linked list is converted to a Red-Black Tree, reducing worst-case bucket lookup from O(n) to O(log n).

The Golden Rule: A good hashCode() implementation distributes keys as uniformly as possible across all buckets, minimizing collisions. Use Objects.hash(field1, field2) for reliable, well-distributed hash codes.

question: HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap vs Hashtable?
answer:
All three implement the Map interface, but differ critically in thread safety, performance, and null handling:


HashMap

  • Thread Safety: ❌ Not thread-safe. Concurrent modification can cause infinite loops (pre-Java 8) or ConcurrentModificationException.
  • Performance: Fastest — zero synchronization overhead.
  • Nulls: ✅ Allows one null key and multiple null values.
  • Use When: Single-threaded code or when access is already externally synchronized.

ConcurrentHashMap

  • Thread Safety: ✅ Uses lock striping (segment-level or bucket-level CAS in Java 8+) instead of locking the entire map.
  • Performance: Near-HashMap performance under high concurrency — multiple threads can read/write different buckets simultaneously.
  • Nulls: ❌ Does NOT allow null keys or values (to avoid ambiguity in concurrent get() returning null).
  • Use When: High-concurrency shared maps (caches, counters, shared registries).

Hashtable

  • Thread Safety: ✅ Entire map locked with synchronized on every operation — blocks all threads on every read or write.
  • Performance: Poor under concurrency due to full lock contention.
  • Nulls: ❌ Does not allow null keys or values.
  • Use When: Never in new code. Legacy class from Java 1.0 — replaced by ConcurrentHashMap.

FeatureHashMapConcurrentHashMapHashtable
Thread-Safe❌✅ (bucket-level)✅ (full lock)
Null Keys✅ One allowed❌❌
Concurrent PerformanceUnsafeExcellent ✅Poor
Recommended?Single-thread✅ Multi-thread❌ Legacy

question: ArrayList vs LinkedList?
answer:
Both implement List, but their underlying data structures produce very different performance characteristics for different operations:


ArrayList — Dynamic Array

  • Structure: Backed by a resizable Object[] array. Elements are stored contiguously in memory.
  • Random Access: O(1) — direct index lookup via array offset. list.get(500) is instant.
  • Add at End: Amortized O(1) — occasional resize doubles capacity and copies the array.
  • Insert/Remove at Middle: O(n) — requires shifting all subsequent elements one position.
  • Memory: Compact — only stores element references + small overhead for unused capacity.

LinkedList — Doubly Linked List

  • Structure: Each element is a Node object holding a value and pointers to the previous and next node.
  • Random Access: O(n) — must traverse from head/tail to reach index. list.get(500) visits 500 nodes.
  • Add/Remove at Known Position (via Iterator): O(1) — only pointer re-linking, no shifting.
  • Add at Head/Tail: O(1) — implements Deque interface, efficient as a queue or stack.
  • Memory: Heavier — each node stores two extra pointers (prev/next references).

OperationArrayListLinkedList
get(index)O(1) ✅O(n) ❌
add() at endO(1) amortized ✅O(1) ✅
add(i, e) middleO(n) ❌O(1) at iterator ✅
Memory usageLower ✅Higher (node overhead)

Rule of Thumb: Default to ArrayList in nearly all situations. Use LinkedList only when you need efficient Deque operations (queue, stack) or frequent insertions at both ends.

question: HashSet vs LinkedHashSet vs TreeSet?
answer:
All three implement Set (no duplicate elements), but differ in ordering and performance:


HashSet

  • Backed By: HashMap internally — keys are the set elements, values are a dummy constant.
  • Ordering: ❌ No guaranteed order — iteration order may differ from insertion order and can change on rehash.
  • Performance: O(1) average for add(), remove(), contains().
  • Nulls: ✅ Allows one null element.
  • Use When: You only need membership testing and don't care about order.

LinkedHashSet

  • Backed By: LinkedHashMap — maintains a doubly-linked list across entries to preserve insertion order.
  • Ordering: ✅ Preserves insertion order during iteration.
  • Performance: Slightly slower than HashSet due to link maintenance overhead, but still O(1) average.
  • Use When: You need fast lookup AND predictable insertion-order iteration (e.g., LRU caches, deduplication with order).

TreeSet

  • Backed By: TreeMap — a Red-Black Tree that keeps elements in sorted order.
  • Ordering: ✅ Maintains natural sorted order (or custom Comparator).
  • Performance: O(log n) for all operations.
  • Nulls: ❌ Does not allow null (throws NullPointerException).
  • Extra Methods: first(), last(), headSet(), tailSet(), floor(), ceiling().
  • Use When: You need sorted elements or range-based queries.

FeatureHashSetLinkedHashSetTreeSet
OrderNoneInsertion orderSorted order
PerformanceO(1) avg ✅O(1) avg ✅O(log n)
Null allowed✅ One✅ One❌ No

question: Checked vs unchecked exceptions?
answer:
Java's exception hierarchy splits into two families, with fundamentally different handling requirements:


Checked Exceptions — Must Handle

  • Definition: Subclass of Exception but NOT RuntimeException.
  • Requirement: The compiler enforces that every checked exception is either caught (try-catch) or declared in the method signature (throws). Failure to do so is a compile-time error.
  • Intent: Represent recoverable, expected failure conditions that callers should explicitly handle.
  • Examples: IOException, SQLException, FileNotFoundException, ParseException.
  • Example Scenario: A file read operation can fail if the file is missing — the caller should decide whether to retry, prompt the user, or use a default.

Unchecked Exceptions — Optional to Handle

  • Definition: Subclass of RuntimeException.
  • Requirement: No compiler enforcement. You may catch them, but are not required to.
  • Intent: Represent programming bugs, invalid state, or precondition violations that should be fixed in code, not caught at runtime.
  • Examples: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, IndexOutOfBoundsException, ClassCastException.

// Checked — compiler forces you to handle it:
try {
    Files.readAllBytes(Path.of("data.txt"));
} catch (IOException e) {
    log.error("File read failed", e);
}

// Unchecked — programming bug, should be fixed:
String name = null;
name.length(); // NullPointerException — fix the null check!

AspectCheckedUnchecked
Parent ClassExceptionRuntimeException
Compiler enforced✅ Yes❌ No
RepresentsRecoverable external failuresProgramming bugs

question: final vs finally vs finalize()?
answer:
These three keywords sound similar but serve completely different purposes across different areas of Java:


final — Keyword (Restriction Modifier)

Applies to variables, methods, and classes to enforce immutability or prevent overriding:

  • final variable: Can only be assigned once. If primitive, value is constant. If reference, the reference is fixed (but the object's internal state may still change).
  • final method: Cannot be overridden by subclasses.
  • final class: Cannot be subclassed. Examples: String, Integer, Math.
final int MAX = 100;       // constant
final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("ok");           // ✅ Allowed — object state changes
list = new ArrayList<>(); // ❌ Compile error — reference is final

finally — Block (Exception Handling)

A block that executes always after a try-catch block, regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught. Used for guaranteed cleanup (closing streams, releasing locks).

try {
    // Risky operation
} catch (IOException e) {
    // Handle error
} finally {
    connection.close(); // Always runs — even on exception or return
}

Note: Prefer try-with-resources over finally for AutoCloseable resources in Java 7+.


finalize() — Method (Deprecated, Do NOT Use)

A method in java.lang.Object that the JVM may call before garbage collecting an object. It was intended for cleanup but is deprecated since Java 9 and removed from Java 18+ because:

  • No guaranteed execution timing — GC may never run it.
  • Can cause GC pauses and object resurrection bugs.
  • Replace with try-with-resources or Cleaner API (Java 9+).

KeywordTypePurpose
finalModifier keywordImmutability / prevent override
finallyException blockGuaranteed cleanup after try-catch
finalize()Object methodDeprecated GC hook — avoid

question: Explain Java Streams: map, filter, flatMap, reduce.
answer:
Java Streams (introduced in Java 8) provide a declarative, functional-style pipeline for processing sequences of data. Streams are lazy — intermediate operations are only executed when a terminal operation is invoked.


Stream Pipeline Structure:

Source → [Intermediate Operations...] → Terminal Operation

1. filter(Predicate) — Selective Pass-Through

Keeps only elements that match the given condition. Analogous to a SQL WHERE clause.

List<Integer> evens = numbers.stream()
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)  // keep even numbers only
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

2. map(Function) — Element Transformation

Transforms each element from one type or value to another. Returns a new stream of transformed elements. Analogous to SQL SELECT column.

List<String> names = users.stream()
    .map(User::getName)      // extract name from each User
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

3. flatMap(Function) — Transform and Flatten

Used when each element maps to a stream of elements (e.g., a list of lists). flatMap merges all sub-streams into a single flat stream.

List<String> allWords = sentences.stream()
    .flatMap(sentence -> Arrays.stream(sentence.split(" ")))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// ["Hello World", "Foo Bar"] → ["Hello", "World", "Foo", "Bar"]

4. reduce(identity, BinaryOperator) — Aggregate to Single Value

Combines all stream elements into a single result using an accumulating function. Analogous to SQL SUM, MAX.

int total = numbers.stream()
    .reduce(0, Integer::sum);  // 0 is identity (initial value)

Optional<Integer> max = numbers.stream()
    .reduce(Integer::max);

OperationTypeInput → OutputSQL Analogy
filterIntermediateStream<T> → Stream<T>WHERE
mapIntermediateStream<T> → Stream<R>SELECT col
flatMapIntermediateStream<Stream<R>> → Stream<R>JOIN + flatten
reduceTerminalStream<T> → TSUM / MAX / MIN

question: What is Optional?
answer:
Optional<T> (introduced in Java 8) is a container object that may or may not contain a non-null value. It provides a type-safe way to express "this method might return nothing" and forces callers to handle the absent case explicitly.


Why Optional was introduced:

Before Optional, methods signaled absence by returning null. Callers often forgot null checks, leading to NullPointerException — the most common Java runtime error. Tony Hoare (inventor of null) called it his "billion-dollar mistake".


Creating an Optional:

Optional<String> full    = Optional.of("hello");    // non-null value
Optional<String> empty   = Optional.empty();        // no value
Optional<String> nullable = Optional.ofNullable(maybeNull); // safe

Consuming an Optional — Safe Patterns:

// 1. orElse — provide a default
String name = optional.orElse("Anonymous");

// 2. orElseGet — lazy default (computed only if needed)
String name = optional.orElseGet(() -> fetchDefaultName());

// 3. orElseThrow — throw if absent
String name = optional.orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException(id));

// 4. map — transform if present, stays Optional
Optional<Integer> len = optional.map(String::length);

// 5. ifPresent — side effect if value exists
optional.ifPresent(name -> log.info("Found user: {}", name));

Anti-Patterns — What NOT to do:

// ❌ NEVER do this — defeats the purpose:
if (optional.isPresent()) {
    String val = optional.get(); // Same as null check!
}

// ❌ Never use Optional as a field or method parameter:
private Optional<String> name; // Use String + @Nullable annotation instead

Rule of Thumb: Use Optional only for method return types where absence is a meaningful, expected outcome. Prefer orElse, map, and orElseThrow over get().

question: Thread vs process?
answer:
A Process and a Thread are the fundamental units of execution in operating systems and JVM environments, but they operate at different levels of resource isolation:


Process — Independent Program Execution

Concept: An isolated instance of an executing program with its own private virtual memory space (Heap, Stack, Code, and File Descriptors).

Isolation: Heavy isolation provided by the Operating System. If one process crashes, other processes remain unaffected.

Communication: Inter-Process Communication (IPC) is required (e.g., sockets, pipes, HTTP, message queues).


Thread — Lightweight Execution Unit

Concept: An execution path within a process. Multiple threads within the same process share the process's Heap memory, Method Area, and file handles, but each thread maintains its own private Call Stack and Program Counter (PC).

Isolation: Low isolation. An unhandled exception or memory leak in one thread can crash or degrade the entire process.

Communication: Inter-Thread Communication is fast via shared heap memory, but requires synchronization mechanisms (locks, volatile, atomic variables) to prevent race conditions.


AttributeProcessThread
Memory AllocationDedicated private memory spaceShares heap & code with process
Creation CostHeavy (OS context allocation)Lightweight
Context Switch TimeSlow (flushes CPU caches & TLB)Fast (shares address space)
Fault ToleranceHigh (isolated)Low (shared memory space)

question: synchronized vs Lock?
answer:
Java provides two primary techniques for mutual exclusion: the built-in synchronized keyword and the flexible java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock API (e.g., ReentrantLock).


synchronized Keyword

Mechanism: Language-level intrinsic monitor lock built into every Java object. Lock acquisition and release are automatic and block-structured.

Pros: Simple syntax, impossible to forget lock release, optimized by JVM (Lock Coarsening, Biased Locking, Lock Elision).

Cons: Unfair by default, non-interruptible, cannot attempt non-blocking lock acquisition (tryLock).


Lock API (ReentrantLock)

Mechanism: Class-based locking framework from j.u.c.locks built on AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS).

Pros: Supports tryLock(timeout), interruptible lock acquisition (lockInterruptibly()), fair ordering options, and multiple condition variables per lock (newCondition()).

Requirement: MUST explicitly release lock in a finally block to avoid permanent deadlocks!


// ReentrantLock Standard Idiom:
Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
lock.lock();
try {
    // Critical Section
} finally {
    lock.unlock(); // Always release in finally block
}

FeaturesynchronizedReentrantLock
Lock ReleaseAutomatic (scope exit)Manual (must use finally)
Non-blocking try❌ No✅ tryLock()
Interruptible❌ No✅ lockInterruptibly()
Fairness option❌ Always non-fair✅ new ReentrantLock(true)

question: What is a race condition?
answer:
A Race Condition occurs in concurrent software when the correctness of a program depends on the relative timing or interleaving of multiple threads executing shared mutable operations.


The Classic Counter Example:

The expression count++ appears to be a single operation, but is actually a 3-step non-atomic sequence:

  1. Read: Read current value of count from main memory into CPU register.
  2. Modify: Increment the register value by 1.
  3. Write: Write the incremented register value back to count in main memory.

Thread A: Read count (10) ----> Increment (11) ------------> Write count (11)
Thread B: ----- Read count (10) -------> Increment (11) -> Write count (11)
// Result: count is 11 instead of expected 12! (Lost Update)

Prevention Strategies:

  • Synchronization: Protect state using synchronized or ReentrantLock.
  • Atomic Classes: Use lock-free primitives like AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicReference (utilizes hardware CAS instructions).
  • Immutability: Make objects immutable so state cannot be modified after construction.
  • Thread Local: Confine variables to a single thread using ThreadLocal.

question: What is deadlock?
answer:
A Deadlock is a concurrency failure where two or more threads are permanently blocked, each waiting for a lock or resource currently held by another thread in the group.


The Four Coffman Conditions (All must hold for a deadlock to occur):

  1. Mutual Exclusion: Resources cannot be shared simultaneously.
  2. Hold and Wait: A thread holding a resource is waiting to acquire another.
  3. No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a thread.
  4. Circular Wait: A closed chain of threads exists, each waiting for a resource held by the next.

// Classic Deadlock Scenario:
// Thread 1 acquires Lock A, then tries to acquire Lock B
// Thread 2 acquires Lock B, then tries to acquire Lock A
Thread 1: synchronized(lockA) { synchronized(lockB) { ... } }
Thread 2: synchronized(lockB) { synchronized(lockA) { ... } }

Best Practices for Deadlock Prevention:

  • Lock Ordering: Always acquire locks in a globally defined, consistent order across all threads.
  • Lock Timeout: Use tryLock(timeout, unit) from ReentrantLock instead of indefinite blocking.
  • Minimize Lock Scope: Hold locks for the shortest possible duration; avoid calling external/unknown code inside locked blocks.
  • Detection Tools: Use jcmd, jstack, or ThreadMXBean (findDeadlockedThreads()) to diagnose deadlocks in production.

question: What does volatile do?
answer:
The volatile keyword in Java provides two core guarantees for thread communication without relying on mutual exclusion locks:


1. Memory Visibility Guarantee

Forces all reads and writes of a volatile variable to go directly to main CPU RAM rather than thread-local CPU L1/L2 caches. When Thread A updates a volatile field, Thread B is guaranteed to see the updated value immediately on its next read.


2. Instruction Reordering Prevention (Happens-Before Relationship)

Prevents the compiler, JIT engine, and CPU hardware from reordering memory reads/writes around the volatile variable. Writing to a volatile variable creates a memory barrier that flushes prior writes.


Crucial Limitation: No Atomicity for Compound Operations!

volatile does NOT make compound operations (e.g., count++ or if (value == 5) value = 6) thread-safe or atomic. For compound operations, use AtomicInteger or synchronized.


// Ideal Use Case: Flag / Shutdown Signal
public class WorkerRunnable implements Runnable {
    private volatile boolean running = true; // Visibility across threads

    public void stop() { running = false; }

    public void run() {
        while (running) {
            // Do work...
        }
    }
}

question: ExecutorService vs manual threads?
answer:
In production Java applications, managing concurrency via the ExecutorService framework is heavily preferred over creating manual new Thread() instances.


Manual Threads (Anti-Pattern in Enterprise Apps)

Creating new Thread(runnable).start() per request has severe drawbacks:

  • High Resource Overhead: Each native OS thread allocates ~1MB stack memory. Creating 1,000 threads consumes ~1GB RAM just for thread stacks.
  • Unbounded Thread Creation: Under traffic spikes, creating threads endlessly triggers java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread.
  • Heavy Context Switching: Managing thousands of active threads causes CPU core trashing and degraded throughput.

ExecutorService (Thread Pooling)

Decouples task submission from thread execution and lifecycle management.

  • Resource Reuse: Reuses a fixed/bounded pool of worker threads.
  • Work Queueing: Incoming tasks beyond pool capacity wait safely in a thread-safe blocking queue.
  • Graceful Lifecycle: Provides structured shutdown (shutdown(), shutdownNow()) and task cancellation via Future.

// Recommended Production Setup:
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
Future<String> future = executor.submit(() -> {
    return "Task completed";
});
String result = future.get(); // Blocking wait for result
executor.shutdown();

question: What is a thread pool?
answer:
A Thread Pool is a managed collection of pre-allocated worker threads that execute tasks asynchronously from a shared work queue.


Core Components of ThreadPoolExecutor:

  1. corePoolSize: Minimum number of threads kept alive in the pool, even if idle.
  2. maximumPoolSize: Maximum allowable threads when the queue fills up.
  3. keepAliveTime: Duration idle non-core threads wait before terminating.
  4. workQueue: BlockingQueue<Runnable> holding pending tasks (e.g., ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue).
  5. RejectedExecutionHandler: Policy triggered when the queue is full and maximumPoolSize is reached.

// Production Configured ThreadPoolExecutor:
ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    10,                                  // Core threads
    50,                                  // Max threads
    60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,               // Keep alive
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000),      // Bounded Work Queue
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // Rejection Policy (Backpressure)
);

Common Rejection Policies:

  • AbortPolicy (Default): Throws RejectedExecutionException.
  • CallerRunsPolicy: Forces the submitting thread to execute the task (creates natural backpressure).
  • DiscardPolicy: Silently drops the task.
  • DiscardOldestPolicy: Drops the oldest unhandled task in queue and retries.

question: Callable and Future?
answer:
In Java concurrency, Callable<V> and Future<V> are the modern abstractions for asynchronous task execution with return values.


Runnable vs Callable

Runnable.run() takes no parameters, returns void, and cannot throw checked exceptions. Callable<V>.call() returns a generic result of type V and can throw checked exceptions.


Future<V> API Key Methods

  • get(): Blocks until computation finishes, then returns the result.
  • get(timeout, unit): Blocks up to specified timeout; throws TimeoutException if exceeded.
  • cancel(mayInterruptIfRunning): Attempts to cancel execution of the task.
  • isDone(): Returns true if task completed (normally, via exception, or cancelled).

Callable<Integer> task = () -> {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
    return 42;
};

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
Future<Integer> future = executor.submit(task);

// Non-blocking work can happen here...

Integer result = future.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // 42
executor.shutdown();

question: Heap vs stack?
answer:
JVM memory management divides memory primarily into Stack Memory and Heap Memory:


Stack Memory — Per-Thread Execution Stack

  • Scope: Private to each thread. Thread A cannot access Thread B's stack.
  • Contents: Local primitive variables and reference pointers pointing to objects residing on the Heap.
  • Lifecycle: LIFO stack frame allocation per method invocation. Pushed on method entry, popped on method return. Automatically reclaimed.
  • Error: Deep or infinite recursion causes java.lang.StackOverflowError.

Heap Memory — Shared Object Store

  • Scope: Global across the entire JVM instance, shared by all threads.
  • Contents: All Java object instances and instance variables (e.g., new User(), new String()).
  • Lifecycle: Reclaimed automatically by the Garbage Collector when objects become unreachable.
  • Error: Exhaustion of memory causes java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space.

FeatureStack MemoryHeap Memory
Thread AccessThread-privateShared across all threads
SpeedExtremely fast (push/pop)Slower (allocation & GC)
LifetimeMethod call durationUntil garbage collected
Error TypeStackOverflowErrorOutOfMemoryError

question: How does Garbage Collection work?
answer:
Garbage Collection (GC) in Java automatically manages heap memory by identifying unreachable objects and reclaiming their memory space.


The Weak Generational Hypothesis

JVM GC algorithms rely on two empirical observations:

  1. Most objects die young (short lived, e.g., temporary variables in a request loop).
  2. Objects that survive past a threshold rarely die soon after.

Generational Memory Subdivisions:

  • Young Generation: Subdivided into Eden Space and two Survivor Spaces (S0, S1). New objects are created in Eden. Minor GC runs frequently here to clean dead objects.
  • Old (Tenured) Generation: Objects that survive multiple Minor GC cycles are promoted to Old Gen. Major/Full GC runs here less frequently.
  • Metaspace (Java 8+): Stores class metadata in native OS memory (replacing old PermGen).

Modern GC Collectors in Production:

  • G1 GC (Garbage-First): Region-based collector for large heaps (4GB+), designed to meet target pause times.
  • ZGC (Z Garbage Collector): Ultra-low latency collector (pause times under 1ms regardless of heap size up to terabytes).

question: What is Spring Framework?
answer:
Spring Framework is the industry-standard, open-source Java enterprise framework centered around Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection (DI).


Core Objectives:

  • Promote loose coupling through interface-driven design.
  • Eliminate boilerplate infrastructure code (database connection setup, transaction management, web mapping).
  • Enable non-invasive programming model (POJOs — Plain Old Java Objects).

Key Spring Modules:

  • Spring Core & Beans: Provides the IoC container and bean management.
  • Spring MVC: Web application framework for REST APIs and HTML views.
  • Spring Data: Simplified persistence layer (JPA, JDBC, Mongo, Redis).
  • Spring Security: Enterprise authentication and authorization framework.
  • Spring AOP: Aspect-Oriented Programming for cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions).

question: What is Dependency Injection?
answer:
Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern implementing Inversion of Control, where an object's dependencies are injected by an external container (Spring IoC) rather than being created inside the class using the new operator.


Comparison: Hardcoded vs Injected

// ❌ Bad: Tightly Coupled (hard to unit test)
public class UserService {
    private UserRepository repo = new UserRepositoryImpl();
}

// ✅ Good: Loose Coupling via Constructor Injection
@Service
public class UserService {
    private final UserRepository repo;

    public UserService(UserRepository repo) {
        this.repo = repo;
    }
}

Benefits of DI:

  • Testability: Mock implementations can easily be passed into constructors during unit tests.
  • Flexibility: Swap implementations (e.g., JpaUserRepository to MongoUserRepository) by changing configuration without modifying business logic.
  • Single Responsibility: Classes focus on their core logic, not on constructing sub-objects.

question: Explain IoC.
answer:
Inversion of Control (IoC) is an architectural principle where the control of object creation, dependency wiring, and lifecycle management is inverted: transferred from custom application code to the Spring IoC Container (ApplicationContext).


The Traditional Flow vs IoC Flow:

  • Traditional: Your code controls the flow — calling constructors, initializing dependencies, and managing object lifecycle.
  • IoC: The framework controls the flow ("Hollywood Principle: Don't call us, we'll call you"). Spring instantiates components, injects dependencies, and triggers lifecycle hooks (@PostConstruct, @PreDestroy).

Spring IoC Containers:

  • BeanFactory: Basic container providing configuration framework and basic bean management.
  • ApplicationContext: Enterprise container extending BeanFactory with AOP integration, i18n message resolution, event publication, and web context capabilities.

question: Component vs Service vs Repository vs Controller?
answer:
All four annotations are stereotype annotations derived from @Component. They register a class as a Spring-managed Bean, but communicate specific architectural roles and carry specialized framework behaviors:


AnnotationArchitectural LayerSpecial Framework Behavior
@ComponentGeneric Spring BeanBasic bean candidate for component scanning
@ServiceBusiness Logic LayerSemantic marker for business services & transactions
@RepositoryPersistence / DAO LayerTranslates native SQL/JPA exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException
@ControllerWeb Presentation LayerHandles HTTP requests; returns view names or REST data (via @ResponseBody)

question: Why prefer constructor injection?
answer:
Spring supports 3 types of dependency injection (Constructor, Field via @Autowired, Setter). Constructor Injection is strongly recommended by the Spring team for 4 critical reasons:


  1. Immutability: Allows dependency fields to be declared as final, ensuring they cannot be mutated after bean construction.
  2. Null-Safety Guarantee: Ensures a bean cannot be instantiated in an incomplete or invalid state — all required dependencies must be provided at construction.
  3. Ease of Unit Testing: Allows easy instantiation in plain JUnit tests without needing Spring container reflection or @MockBean annotations.
  4. Circular Dependency Prevention: Spring detects circular dependencies at startup time during constructor calls, failing fast rather than failing unexpectedly later.

question: What is a Spring Bean?
answer:
A Spring Bean is an object that is instantiated, configured, assembled, and managed by the Spring Inversion of Control (IoC) container (ApplicationContext).


Bean Definition Sources:

  • Component Scanning: Annotating classes with @Component, @Service, @Repository, or @RestController.
  • Java Configuration: Methods annotated with @Bean inside a @Configuration class.
  • XML Configuration: Legacy <bean id="..." class="..."/> definitions.

question: What are Bean scopes?
answer:
Spring Bean Scopes control the lifecycle and instance creation strategy of a bean within the ApplicationContext:


ScopeDescription
singleton (Default)One single shared bean instance per Spring ApplicationContext. Cached for subsequent lookups.
prototypeCreates a brand new bean instance every time it is requested from the container.
request (Web)One bean instance created per HTTP request lifecycle. Discarded on request completion.
session (Web)One bean instance per HTTP Session.
application (Web)One bean instance per ServletContext.

question: Explain Spring Bean lifecycle.
answer:
The Spring Bean Lifecycle consists of distinct creation, initialization, usage, and destruction phases managed by the container:


  1. Instantiation: Container constructs bean via constructor or factory method.
  2. Populate Properties: Container injects dependencies via setters/fields/constructors.
  3. Aware Callbacks: Container calls Aware interfaces if implemented (e.g., BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware).
  4. BeanPostProcessor (Pre-Initialization): Executes postProcessBeforeInitialization() across all custom processors.
  5. Initialization: Executes custom init methods (e.g., @PostConstruct, InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()).
  6. BeanPostProcessor (Post-Initialization): Executes postProcessAfterInitialization(). AOP proxies (for @Transactional, @Async) are created here!
  7. Ready for Use: Bean is fully configured and served to application code.
  8. Destruction: On container shutdown, calls @PreDestroy or DisposableBean.destroy().

question: What is @Autowired?
answer:
@Autowired is an annotation that instructs Spring's dependency injection engine to automatically wire a matching bean by type into a constructor, setter method, or field.


Resolving Ambiguity:

If multiple beans implement the target interface, Spring throws an NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Resolve ambiguity using:

  • @Qualifier("beanName"): Specifies exact bean name to inject.
  • @Primary: Marks a bean class as default choice among candidates.

Note: Since Spring 4.3, classes with a single constructor do not require an explicit @Autowired annotation.

question: What is Spring AOP?
answer:
Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) complements Object-Oriented Programming by separating cross-cutting concerns (logging, security checks, transaction management, performance metrics) from core business logic using dynamic proxy wrapping.


Key AOP Terminology:

  • Aspect: A module encapsulating a cross-cutting concern (e.g., LoggingAspect).
  • Join Point: A point during program execution (in Spring AOP, always a method execution).
  • Advice: Action taken by an aspect at a Join Point (@Before, @After, @Around, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing).
  • Pointcut: A predicate expression matching Join Points (e.g., execution(* com.service.*.*(..))).

question: Spring vs Spring Boot?
answer:
Spring Framework provides core enterprise infrastructure (DI, IoC, AOP, Data, MVC), while Spring Boot is an opinionated framework built on top of Spring to eliminate boilerplate configuration and streamline application bootstrap.


FeatureSpring FrameworkSpring Boot
ConfigurationManual Java/XML configuration requiredAuto-configuration based on classpath JARs
Server DeploymentExport WAR & deploy to external Tomcat/WildFlyEmbedded server (Tomcat/Jetty) → Executable JAR
Dependency ManagementManual specification of individual library versionsStarter dependencies with curated version BOMs
Production MetricsMust configure metrics/health manuallyBuilt-in Actuator endpoints (health, metrics, env)

question: What does @SpringBootApplication contain?
answer:
@SpringBootApplication is a meta-annotation that combines three core Spring annotations into a single convenience declaration on the main application class:


  • @SpringBootConfiguration: A specialized form of @Configuration designating the class as a primary source of bean definitions.
  • @EnableAutoConfiguration: Activates Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism, analyzing classpath dependencies to automatically register beans.
  • @ComponentScan: Scans the current package and all sub-packages for Spring components (@Component, @Service, @Repository, @RestController).

// Standard Spring Boot Entry Point:
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}

question: What is auto-configuration?
answer:
Auto-configuration is Spring Boot's mechanism for automatically configuring application beans based on JAR dependencies present on the classpath, system properties, and existing user-defined beans.


How Auto-Configuration Works:

  1. Spring Boot inspects AutoConfiguration.imports (or legacy META-INF/spring.factories) from starter JARs.
  2. Evaluates conditional annotations to determine if a bean should be registered:
    • @ConditionalOnClass: Executes only if a specific class is present on the classpath (e.g., HikariDataSource.class).
    • @ConditionalOnMissingBean: Executes only if the user hasn't already declared a custom bean of that type (allows user overrides!).
    • @ConditionalOnProperty: Executes only if a configuration property matches (e.g., spring.datasource.url).

question: What are Spring Boot starters?
answer:
Spring Boot Starters are curated dependency descriptors that bundle related libraries, transitive dependencies, and version management into a single convenient import for build tools (Maven/Gradle).


Popular Official Starters:

  • spring-boot-starter-web: Spring MVC, REST controllers, Jackson JSON, and embedded Tomcat.
  • spring-boot-starter-data-jpa: Spring Data JPA, Hibernate ORM, HikariCP connection pool, and Jakarta Persistence.
  • spring-boot-starter-security: Spring Security core filters, password encoders, and authentication configs.
  • spring-boot-starter-test: JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, Hamcrest, and Spring Test context.

question: How does embedded Tomcat work?
answer:
Spring Boot packages an embedded Servlet container (Tomcat by default via spring-boot-starter-web) directly inside the executable JAR file.


Under the Hood Execution Flow:

  1. When main() runs, SpringApplication.run() initializes a ServletWebServerApplicationContext.
  2. It detects TomcatServletWebServerFactory on the classpath.
  3. Spring programmatically instantiates Tomcat, configures HTTP ports, registers the DispatcherServlet, and starts the server instance.
  4. The application runs as a standalone Java process without needing external application server installation (WAR deployment).

question: How do you create a REST API?
answer:
A production-ready Spring Boot REST API incorporates controller mapping, request validation, service delegation, and DTO responses:


@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/users")
public class UserController {
    private final UserService userService;

    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<UserDTO> createUser(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        UserDTO response = userService.createUser(request);
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(response);
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDTO> getUserById(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(userService.getUserById(id));
    }
}

question: @Controller vs @RestController?
answer:
Both annotations mark web controllers in Spring MVC, but differ in their default response serialization model:


  • @Controller: Designed for traditional web applications. Controller methods return a String representing a view name (e.g., Thymeleaf/JSP template path).
  • @RestController: A convenience meta-annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. Methods return domain objects or ResponseEntity directly serialized to JSON/XML by Jackson.

// @RestController is syntactic sugar for:
@Controller
@ResponseBody
public class UserApiController { ... }

question: @RequestParam vs @PathVariable vs @RequestBody?
answer:
These three annotations extract different parts of an incoming HTTP request into method parameters:


AnnotationSource LocationExample URI / Payload
@PathVariableURI Template path segments/users/{id} → /users/42
@RequestParamURL query parameters/users?page=1&size=10
@RequestBodyHTTP request body payloadJSON object {"name": "Alice"}

question: How handle exceptions globally?
answer:
In Spring Boot, handle exceptions centrally across all controllers using @RestControllerAdvice paired with @ExceptionHandler methods:


@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleNotFound(UserNotFoundException ex) {
        ErrorResponse error = new ErrorResponse(
            "NOT_FOUND",
            ex.getMessage(),
            LocalDateTime.now()
        );
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(error);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> handleValidation(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
        Map<String, String> errors = new HashMap<>();
        ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().forEach(err ->
            errors.put(err.getField(), err.getDefaultMessage())
        );
        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(errors);
    }
}

question: What is @ControllerAdvice?
answer:
@ControllerAdvice is a component annotation for intercepting and applying cross-cutting logic across all controllers in a Spring application.


Capabilities:

  • Global Exception Handling: @ExceptionHandler methods.
  • Global Model Attributes: @ModelAttribute methods to add common data to all view models.
  • Global Init Binder: @InitBinder methods to customize data binding and formatting globally.

@RestControllerAdvice is simply @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody.

question: How perform validation?
answer:
Input validation in Spring Boot uses Jakarta Bean Validation (JSR-380 / Hibernate Validator) annotations on DTO fields, triggered by @Valid on controller methods:


// 1. DTO with Constraints:
public class CreateUserRequest {
    @NotBlank(message = "Username is required")
    @Size(min = 3, max = 20, message = "Must be 3-20 characters")
    private String username;

    @NotBlank(message = "Email is required")
    @Email(message = "Invalid email format")
    private String email;

    @Min(value = 18, message = "Must be at least 18 years old")
    private int age;
}

// 2. Controller with @Valid:
@PostMapping("/users")
public ResponseEntity<Void> createUser(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
    userService.save(request);
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).build();
}

question: What are @Valid and validation annotations?
answer:
@Valid (from Jakarta Validation) triggers recursive validation on an object graph. Common constraint annotations include:


AnnotationConstraint Description
@NotNullValue must not be null (allows empty strings/collections).
@NotEmptyMust not be null AND size/length > 0.
@NotBlankString must not be null AND trimmed length > 0.
@Pattern(regex=...)String must match specified regular expression.
@Min / @MaxNumeric value boundaries.

question: How configure dev/test/prod?
answer:
Spring Boot manages multi-environment configurations using Spring Profiles (e.g., dev, test, prod):


  • Profile Files: application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml.
  • Activation Methods:
    • Environment variable: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
    • JVM parameter: -Dspring.profiles.active=dev
    • In configuration: spring.profiles.active=local
  • Conditional Beans: Annotate components with @Profile("dev") to load beans only in specific active profiles (e.g., in-memory H2 database for dev vs PostgreSQL for prod).

question: application.properties vs YAML?
answer:
Both formats configure Spring Boot properties, but differ in syntax flexibility and features:


Featureapplication.propertiesapplication.yml (YAML)
SyntaxFlat key-value (e.g., spring.db.url=...)Hierarchical tree with indentation
Lists / ArraysIndexed keys servers[0]=aClean list bullet syntax (- serverA)
Multi-documentRequires separate files per profileMulti-profile blocks in single file (---)

question: What is Actuator?
answer:
Spring Boot Actuator provides production-ready operational management features for monitoring application health, metrics, environment details, and thread diagnostics via HTTP/JMX endpoints.


Key Actuator Endpoints:

  • /actuator/health: Shows application health status (DB connectivity, disk space).
  • /actuator/metrics: Exposes Micrometer metrics (JVM heap usage, HTTP response times).
  • /actuator/prometheus: Formats metrics for Prometheus scraping.
  • /actuator/loggers: Allows viewing and dynamically changing log levels at runtime without restarting!

question: Authentication vs authorization?
answer:
Security enforcement splits into two core phases:


ConceptCore QuestionExample Mechanism
Authentication (AuthN)Who are you?Verifying username/password, JWT signature, OAuth2 token
Authorization (AuthZ)Are you allowed to do this?Checking if user has ROLE_ADMIN before allowing DELETE /user/42

question: Where should a JWT be stored?
answer:
Storage strategy directly affects vulnerability to XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) and CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) attacks:


  • localStorage / sessionStorage: ❌ Vulnerable to XSS. Any malicious script or compromised npm package running on the domain can steal tokens from localStorage.
  • HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite Cookie: ✅ Recommended for Web Apps. HttpOnly prevents JavaScript access (mitigating XSS theft); SameSite=Strict mitigates CSRF.

question: What happens when JWT expires?
answer:
When an Access Token expires, the server returns 401 Unauthorized with an EXPIRED_TOKEN error code.


The Refresh Token Pattern:

  1. Access Token: Short-lived (e.g., 15 minutes) for API authorization.
  2. Refresh Token: Long-lived (e.g., 7 days) stored securely in HttpOnly cookie or database.
  3. When Access Token expires, the client's HTTP interceptor silently calls POST /api/auth/refresh with the Refresh Token to obtain a fresh Access Token without requiring user re-login.

question: What is Security Filter Chain?
answer:
The SecurityFilterChain is an ordered sequence of Spring Security Servlet Filters that inspect every incoming HTTP request to handle CORS, CSRF, authentication, authorization, and session creation.


Key Standard Filters in Order:

  1. CorsFilter: Handles cross-origin preflight requests.
  2. CsrfFilter: Validates CSRF tokens.
  3. UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter: Processes form logins.
  4. BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter / Custom JwtFilter: Extracts and validates JWTs.
  5. AuthorizationFilter: Enforces URL-based role & permission rules.

question: How secure specific endpoints?
answer:
Spring Security 5.7+ configures endpoint security via a SecurityFilterChain bean:


@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@EnableMethodSecurity // Enables @PreAuthorize
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/api/v1/auth/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/v1/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/api/v1/**").hasAuthority("DELETE_PERM")
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .build();
    }
}

question: Roles vs authorities?
answer:
In Spring Security, GrantedAuthority is the core interface representing individual user permissions:


  • Authority (Granular Permission): Fine-grained permission strings (e.g., READ_DOCUMENT, DELETE_USER). Checked via hasAuthority('READ_DOCUMENT').
  • Role (Permission Group): A high-level group of authorities. In Spring Security, a Role is simply an authority prefixed with ROLE_. hasRole('ADMIN') automatically looks for GrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN").

question: How implement refresh tokens?
answer:
A robust Refresh Token architecture decouples short-lived access authorization from long-lived session management:


  1. Token Pair Generation: Upon successful login, the auth server issues a short-lived Access Token (15 mins) and a cryptographically secure Refresh Token (7 days).
  2. Secure Storage: Store the Refresh Token in a database table containing user_id, hashed_token, device_info, ip_address, expires_at, and is_revoked.
  3. Token Rotation: Every time a Refresh Token is used to get a new Access Token, invalidate the old Refresh Token and issue a brand new pair.
  4. Remote Revocation: If a Refresh Token is reused after revocation (signaling theft), immediately revoke ALL active refresh tokens for that user account.

question: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN vs RIGHT JOIN?
answer:
SQL JOIN operations combine rows from two or more tables based on a related matching key column:


JOIN TypeReturned RowsUnmatched Rows Behavior
INNER JOINOnly matching rows from BOTH tablesDiscarded from result set
LEFT JOINALL rows from Left table + matching Right table rowsFills NULL for unmatched Right columns
RIGHT JOINALL rows from Right table + matching Left table rowsFills NULL for unmatched Left columns
FULL OUTER JOINALL rows from BOTH tablesFills NULL whenever a match is absent

question: What is an index?
answer:
A database Index is a specialized data structure (typically a B+ Tree or Hash Index) maintained alongside a database table to accelerate data retrieval operations.


Analogy: Similar to an index at the back of a textbook — allows finding specific topics directly without reading every page from start to finish (Table Scan).


Key Advantages:

  • Transforms full table scans (O(N) sequential reads) into fast logarithmic lookups (O(log N) tree traversals).
  • Enforces data uniqueness (Unique Indexes).
  • Accelerates JOIN, WHERE, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY clauses.

question: When can an index hurt performance?
answer:
While indexes speed up reads, improper indexing can severely degrade database performance:


  • Write Overhead: Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must update both the table data pages and all associated index B+ Trees. Too many indexes slow down write operations.
  • Low Selectivity Columns: Indexing columns with few unique values (e.g., gender or status_flag) causes the query planner to ignore the index in favor of sequential scans.
  • Storage Overhead: Indexes consume disk space and RAM buffer pool space.
  • Overlapping / Duplicate Composite Indexes: Indexing (A, B) makes a standalone index on (A) redundant due to the Leftmost Prefix Rule.

question: Explain ACID.
answer:
ACID defines the four core properties guaranteed by relational database transaction management engines (e.g., InnoDB, PostgreSQL):


PropertyDefinitionImplementation Mechanism
Atomicity"All or Nothing" — every statement in a transaction succeeds or all are rolled back.Undo Log
ConsistencyDatabase transitions from one valid state to another, upholding all constraints & foreign keys.Schema validation & constraints
IsolationConcurrent transactions execute without dirty reads or interference.Locks & MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)
DurabilityOnce committed, changes survive permanently even during power outages or system crashes.Redo Log / Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

question: What is normalization?
answer:
Database Normalization is the process of structuring relational database schemas to eliminate data redundancy and prevent data modification anomalies (Insert, Update, Delete anomalies).


  • 1NF (First Normal Form): Atomic values (no multi-valued columns or nested arrays).
  • 2NF (Second Normal Form): Meets 1NF + all non-key columns fully depend on the entire Primary Key (eliminates partial dependency).
  • 3NF (Third Normal Form): Meets 2NF + no non-key column depends on another non-key column (eliminates transitive dependency).

Denormalization: Intentionally introducing redundant data in read-heavy or analytical systems (data warehouses) to eliminate expensive JOIN operations and boost read speeds.

question: What is a transaction?
answer:
A Database Transaction is a sequence of SQL operations executed as a single, indivisible logical unit of work that upholds ACID properties.


BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT; -- Both updates saved atomically!
-- If an error occurs, ROLLBACK reverts all changes.

question: WHERE vs HAVING?
answer:
Both clauses filter data in SQL queries, but operate at different stages of query execution:


ClauseFiltering StageAggregate Functions Allowed?
WHEREFilters individual rows BEFORE GROUP BY aggregation.❌ Cannot contain aggregates (e.g., COUNT(), SUM())
HAVINGFilters aggregated groups AFTER GROUP BY aggregation.✅ Can filter aggregate values (e.g., HAVING COUNT(*) > 5)

SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) 
FROM employees 
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'       -- 1. Filter rows first
GROUP BY department_id 
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;        -- 2. Filter aggregated groups second

question: Primary key vs foreign key vs unique key?
answer:
Quick Answer:
  • Primary Key: Uniquely identifies a row; NOT NULL; exactly one per table.
  • Foreign Key: References a Primary/Unique Key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.
  • Unique Key: Enforces uniqueness across values in a column; allows NULL values depending on DB vendor.

question: How optimize a slow SQL query?
answer:
Quick Answer: Optimize slow queries systematically:
  1. Inspect EXPLAIN ANALYZE query execution plan.
  2. Add missing indexes on JOIN, WHERE, and ORDER BY columns.
  3. Avoid SELECT *; request only required columns.
  4. Eliminate N+1 queries using JOINs/fetch joins.

question: Database deadlock and prevention?
answer: Quick Answer: A database deadlock occurs when Transaction A holds Lock 1 waiting for Lock 2, while Transaction B holds Lock 2 waiting for Lock 1. Prevent by accessing tables in a fixed uniform order and keeping transactions short.

question: JPA vs Hibernate?
answer: Quick Answer: JPA (Java Persistence API) is a standard specification defining object-relational mapping interfaces, whereas Hibernate is an actual implementation library of that specification.

question: save vs saveAndFlush vs flush?
answer:
Quick Answer:
  • save(): Persists entity into the Spring Data persistence context (SQL may be deferred until transaction commit).
  • flush(): Immediately executes pending SQL statements to the database within the current transaction without committing.
  • saveAndFlush(): Combines save() and flush() in one call.

question: @Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue?
answer:
Quick Answer:
  • @Entity: Marks a Java class as a JPA persistent entity mapped to a DB table.
  • @Id: Designates the primary key property.
  • @GeneratedValue: Configures primary key generation strategy (IDENTITY, SEQUENCE, AUTO).

question: One-to-One, One-to-Many, Many-to-Many?
answer:
Quick Answer:
  • @OneToOne: 1 parent maps to 1 child.
  • @OneToMany / @ManyToOne: 1 parent maps to multiple children (most common).
  • @ManyToMany: Maps many-to-many via a join table. Always define ownership using mappedBy.

question: Lazy vs Eager loading?
answer: Quick Answer: Lazy Loading (FetchType.LAZY) fetches associated entities on-demand when accessed, avoiding unnecessary data retrieval. Eager Loading (FetchType.EAGER) fetches associations immediately with the parent query.

question: What is N+1?
answer: Quick Answer: The N+1 Select Problem occurs when loading 1 query for N parent entities triggers N additional separate queries to fetch related child entities, causing severe performance degradation (1 + N = 101 queries for 100 rows!).

question: How solve N+1?
answer:
Quick Answer: Solve N+1 using:
  • JOIN FETCH in JPQL / HQL: SELECT p FROM Parent p JOIN FETCH p.children.
  • @EntityGraph annotation.
  • @BatchSize(size = 25) on collection mappings.

question: Hibernate first-level cache?
answer: Quick Answer: The First-Level Cache is the Hibernate Session / EntityManager cache enabled by default. It caches entity instances within the scope of a single transaction, preventing duplicate SELECT queries for the same entity ID.

question: What is @Transactional?
answer: Quick Answer: @Transactional marks method/class boundaries for automatic transaction management using Spring AOP proxies, opening a transaction before execution and committing/rolling back upon completion.

question: Exception inside @Transactional?
answer: Quick Answer: By default, Spring rolls back @Transactional only for Unchecked Exceptions (RuntimeException and Error). Checked exceptions do NOT trigger rollback unless configured with @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class).

question: What makes an API RESTful?
answer: Quick Answer: A RESTful API adheres to REST architectural constraints: Resource identification via URIs, Stateless interactions, Standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), Proper HTTP status codes, and JSON/XML representations.

question: GET vs POST vs PUT vs PATCH vs DELETE?
answer:
Quick Answer:
  • GET: Read resource (Safe & Idempotent).
  • POST: Create new resource (Non-Idempotent).
  • PUT: Completely replace resource (Idempotent).
  • PATCH: Partial update (Idempotent when implemented properly).
  • DELETE: Remove resource (Idempotent).

question: Explain 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 500.
answer:
Quick Answer:
  • 200 OK: Success.
  • 201 Created: Resource created.
  • 400 Bad Request: Invalid request validation.
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing/invalid credentials.
  • 403 Forbidden: Authenticated but unauthorized.
  • 404 Not Found: Resource missing.
  • 409 Conflict: Unique constraint conflict.
  • 500 Internal Error: Unexpected server exception.

question: What is idempotency?
answer: Quick Answer: Idempotency means executing the exact same request multiple times produces the identical side-effect as executing it once. Use client-generated Idempotency-Key headers for payment endpoints.

question: How design a scalable REST API?
answer: Quick Answer: Scale REST APIs using Stateless application instances behind a Load Balancer, Redis caching, DB Read-Replicas, Connection Pooling (HikariCP), Offset/Cursor Pagination, and Asynchronous Queue Processing.

question: How implement pagination?
answer: Quick Answer: Implement pagination using Offset Pagination (page=2&size=20) for small datasets or Cursor / Keyset Pagination (after_id=1050) for large/changing datasets to prevent degraded OFFSET query performance.

question: What is API versioning?
answer: Quick Answer: Version APIs to prevent breaking changes: URI Versioning (/api/v1/users), Request Header (X-API-Version: 1), or Accept Header Media Types.

question: Monolith vs microservices?
answer: Quick Answer: A Monolith is built and deployed as a single application unit. Microservices decompose functionality into independent, domain-driven services that scale and deploy independently over the network.

question: When should you NOT use microservices?
answer:
Quick Answer: Avoid microservices when:
  • Domain boundaries are unclear or team size is small (< 10 devs).
  • DevOps infrastructure, CI/CD, and distributed tracing observability are missing.
  • High distributed network latency and eventual consistency overhead cannot be tolerated.

question: How do microservices communicate?
answer: Quick Answer: Microservices communicate Synchronously via REST HTTP/gRPC (immediate response needed) or Asynchronously via Message Brokers like Apache Kafka / RabbitMQ (event-driven, decoupled).

question: What is service discovery?
answer: Quick Answer: Service Discovery (e.g., Netflix Eureka, HashiCorp Consul, Kubernetes DNS) dynamically tracks network IP addresses and ports of healthy microservice instances as they scale up or down.

question: Circuit breaker?
answer: Quick Answer: A Circuit Breaker (Resilience4j) prevents cascading service failures by wrapping downstream calls. It transitions between Closed (normal), Open (failing fast without calling downstream), and Half-Open (testing recovery).

question: What is Docker?
answer: Quick Answer: Docker packages an application and its entire runtime environment into a lightweight, portable container image that runs consistently across dev, test, and production OS environments.

question: Image vs container?
answer: Quick Answer: A Docker Image is an immutable read-only template file containing application code and dependencies, whereas a Container is a runnable isolated instance of an image.

question: What is a Dockerfile?
answer:
Quick Answer: A Dockerfile is a text script containing commands (FROM, COPY, RUN, EXPOSE, ENTRYPOINT) used to build a Docker image. 
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/app.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

question: How Dockerize Spring Boot?
answer: Quick Answer: Dockerize Spring Boot using Multi-stage Docker builds to compile with Maven/Gradle in stage 1 and copy only the final slim JAR into a lightweight JRE base image in stage 2.

question: AWS services for Java apps?
answer:
Quick Answer: Common AWS Services for Java Apps:
  • Compute: EC2, ECS (Elastic Container Service), EKS (Kubernetes), AWS Lambda.
  • Database: RDS (Aurora/PostgreSQL), DynamoDB.
  • Storage & Auth: S3, IAM, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch.

question: EC2 vs ECS vs Lambda?
answer: Quick Answer: EC2 = Virtual Server (Full OS Control); ECS = Container Orchestrator; Lambda = Serverless Event-driven Function with zero server management.

question: What is S3?
answer: Quick Answer: Amazon S3 is high-durability object storage for files (images, PDFs, logs). Applications store file metadata in a relational database and stream actual file bytes to S3 buckets via Pre-signed URLs.

question: How deploy Spring Boot to AWS?
answer: Quick Answer: Deploy Spring Boot to AWS by building a Docker image -> Pushing to AWS ECR -> Deploying container tasks to AWS ECS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) connected to AWS RDS PostgreSQL.

question: API suddenly becomes very slow. What do you investigate?
answer:
Quick Answer: Debug slow APIs following the systematic order:
  1. Inspect APM traces/metrics to isolate latency (App vs DB vs Downstream API).
  2. Check CPU, Memory, GC pauses, and thread pool exhaustion.
  3. Check DB connection pool (HikariCP) and slow query logs.

question: Spring Boot app uses 90% CPU. What do you check?
answer: Quick Answer: For 90% CPU spikes: Capture thread dumps using jstack or async-profiler to identify busy threads, inspect GC logs for frequent Full GC pauses, and check for infinite loops or expensive regex execution.

question: SQL query takes 5 seconds. How optimize?
answer: Quick Answer: Optimize a 5-second SQL query: Capture query parameters, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, add composite indexes matching WHERE/JOIN columns, avoid functions on indexed columns, and eliminate N+1 subqueries.

question: API receives 10,000 requests/sec. How scale?
answer: Quick Answer: Scale for 10,000 req/sec: Make service stateless -> Deploy horizontal instances behind Load Balancer -> Cache hot data in Redis -> Use DB Read-Replicas -> Use Kafka for async processing.

question: Two users update same record. Prevent inconsistency?
answer: Quick Answer: Prevent concurrent update conflicts using Optimistic Locking (@Version column) for low-conflict scenarios or Pessimistic Locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) for high-contention rules.

question: Downstream microservice is down. What should happen?
answer: Quick Answer: When downstream services fail: Trigger Resilience4j Circuit Breakers to fail-fast, return fallback responses or cached data, and queue non-critical events asynchronously.

question: Production 500 errors cannot be reproduced locally. Debug?
answer: Quick Answer: Debug un-reproducible 500 errors by analyzing centralized logs (ELK/Datadog) correlated via distributed Tracing IDs (Micrometer Tracing/Zipkin) and reproducing with sanitized production-like data.

question: Customer submits payment twice. Prevent duplicates?
answer: Quick Answer: Prevent duplicate payments using client-supplied Idempotency Keys stored in Redis/DB with unique constraints, ensuring repeated requests return original cached transaction results.

question: Database goes down. How should app behave?
answer: Quick Answer: When DB goes down: Fail fast with 503 Service Unavailable, configure HikariCP connection timeouts to prevent thread starvation, and auto-recover when DB comes back online.

question: OutOfMemoryError. How investigate?
answer: Quick Answer: Investigate OutOfMemoryError by generating heap dumps (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError), analyzing leak suspects in Eclipse MAT, checking GC logs, and identifying memory-leaking static maps or unclosed streams.

question: Logging and monitoring in production?
answer: Quick Answer: Production Observability: Structured JSON logging with traceId/spanId, Prometheus metrics for Golden Signals (Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation), and Grafana alerts on SLO thresholds.

question: Design a URL shortener.
answer:
Quick Answer: URL Shortener Architecture:
  • POST /shorten: Takes long URL -> Generates Base62 7-char hash -> Saves (shortKey, longUrl) in DB -> Returns short link.
  • GET /{shortKey}: Checks Redis Cache -> On miss queries DB -> Returns 302 Found redirect to original long URL.
